title: Gemini Robotics 2.5 hits 96 percent success sorting parts on a Mercedes-Benz line
subtitle: Google DeepMind's model, running on Apptronik's Apollo 2 humanoid, completed an automotive kitting task across more than 200 variants at active plants in Hungary and Germany. DeepMind says moving from 96 to human-level reliability is a steep road.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Google DeepMind announced Gemini Robotics 2.5 and reported a 96 percent success rate in a Mercedes-Benz proof-of-concept run on Apptronik's Apollo 2 humanoid. The pilot took place on active production lines in Kecskemét, Hungary and Sindelfingen, Germany, and the specific task was automotive kitting: picking metal vehicle brackets out of collection bins, identifying each part, and placing them in sequencing bins in the order the next vehicle on the line requires. Across more than 200 task variants, DeepMind reports 30 to 100 percent success depending on the task and 20 to 30 percent faster completion than the prior Gemini Robotics generation. The model is rolling out to Google's robotics partners now, and Mercedes-Benz has not announced any purchase of Apollo fleets. DeepMind's robotics director called the gap from 96 percent to near-human reliability a steep road.

The 96 percent figure is more important than it sounds and less important than it looks. Automotive assembly tasks have historically been the domain of highly engineered fixed robots with sub-millimeter precision and no tolerance for perception errors. A general-purpose humanoid running a multimodal foundation model is a different animal: it is slower, more expensive per unit, and less reliable on any single task than a dedicated jig — but it can be reconfigured by instruction instead of by retooling. Mercedes did not run this trial because Apollo is cheaper than a KUKA arm; they ran it because kitting is one of the places on a modern vehicle line that still relies on humans doing fiddly, variant-heavy work. If Apollo can clear a reliability bar close enough to a human operator, the labor and ergonomics math changes before the unit economics do.

This sits inside a broader humanoid cycle that finally has shippable work to show. Figure, Agility Robotics (which went public via SPAC last month), 1X, Boston Dynamics, Sanctuary AI, and Apptronik have all run factory or warehouse pilots in the last six months, and the current benchmark is no longer whether the robot can walk but how long it can run a production shift without a reset. Gemini Robotics 2.5 also marks a design change for DeepMind: the model targets what the team calls commercially useful tasks as a primary metric, which is what gets Mercedes to open its lines to a camera. Expect the next twelve months to be dominated by pilot-to-production announcements from auto, logistics, and electronics manufacturing, and expect the losers to be the humanoid programs that cannot show measured success rates on named sites.

A takeaway for learners: in robotics, benchmarks on live production lines beat benchmarks on demo stages. When you read a humanoid announcement, ask three questions — what is the exact task, where did it run, and what is the measured success rate — and discount any claim that cannot answer all three. DeepMind's willingness to publish a 96 percent figure with a named site and named partner is the standard the field should hold itself to. If you want to work in this area, build a habit of reproducing that scrutiny: pull the task spec, estimate the human baseline, and treat anything without a site name and a number the way you would treat a benchmark run on a synthetic eval.
